common_name: Keukett Buckwheat (Cornell/Birkett Mills-Bred Northeast Grain Buckwheat)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill shallowly into warm soil any time after the last frost, since this variety establishes quickly and can be succession-sown through midsummer.

directions: Keukett is a buckwheat selection released from a Cornell University breeding program and licensed to the Birkett Mills, developed specifically to give Northeast growers a more productive alternative to older varieties like Manor. It shows vigorous early-season growth and notably better lodging resistance than older cultivars, helping more of the crop stand through to harvest rather than falling over as it matures. Broadcast or drill into a warm, well-worked seedbed after frost danger has passed, then mow or incorporate at first bloom if growing it strictly as a soil-building cover rather than for grain. Because the stand resists lodging well, it can also be left slightly longer to maximize pollinator forage before termination.
sources: Cornell University Horticulture Section — Buckwheat Growers Guide

common_name: Rackmaster Trophy Radish (Pennington Daikon-Type Food Plot and Cover Crop Radish)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill 6 to 10 weeks before the first fall frost so the taproot and leafy top have time to size up before winterkill.

directions: Rackmaster Trophy Radish is a daikon-type forage radish marketed by Pennington primarily for wildlife food plots but agronomically functions as a standard tillage radish, producing a deep taproot alongside heavy leafy top growth. Drill or broadcast into a firm seedbed in late summer so plants reach a full rosette and root mass before a hard freeze, since the crop is intended to winterkill and decompose rather than overwinter. The decomposing root channels loosen compacted soil and improve water infiltration, while the breakdown of tissue releases scavenged nitrogen and minerals back into the topsoil ahead of a following planting. Because the foliage is highly palatable, stands grown in areas with heavy deer or wildlife pressure may need larger plantings to offset grazing before the root fully matures.
sources: Pennington Seed — Rackmaster Trophy Radishes product information

common_name: Pink Candles Nanking Cherry (Self-Pollinating Pink-Flowered Bush Cherry)

planting.note: Set container or bare-root shrubs out in early spring once soil is workable, in full sun with good drainage.

directions: Pink Candles is a named Nanking cherry selection whose stems are completely smothered in bright pink blossoms in early spring before the fuzzy foliage emerges, making it as much a flowering ornamental as a fruiting shrub. Unlike the species type, which generally needs a second seedling nearby for cross-pollination, Pink Candles is self-fruitful and will set a crop of small, sweet, deep-red cherries on a single plant. Fruit ripens in late summer and is best used fresh or cooked into jelly and preserves rather than shipped, since it is soft and perishable. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and prune lightly right after harvest since the shrub flowers and fruits on the previous year's wood.

planting.note: Start indoors under warmth and bright light about a month before the last frost, then transplant once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees.

directions: Eleonora was selected as one of the first Genovese-type sweet basils to carry intermediate resistance to downy mildew, a fungal disease that has become a major problem for basil growers worldwide. Its leaves are medium green, slightly serrated, and somewhat narrower and flatter than old-style Genovese basil, but the flavor remains classic sweet basil for pesto and fresh use. Pinch out flower spikes regularly to keep plants bushy and productive, and grow in full sun with even moisture and good airflow to further reduce disease pressure. It performs well in both field rows and container production.

common_name: Green Globe Basil (Compact Italian Bush Basil)

planting.note: Start seed indoors a month or so before the last frost and set out once the soil and nights have warmed, or direct sow after frost danger passes.

directions: Known in Italy as Finissimo Verde a Palla, Green Globe forms dense, perfectly rounded little bushes of small, spicy-sweet leaves that look tidy without any pruning or shearing. Its compact, uniform globe habit makes it a favorite for edging, pots, and formal herb-garden borders as well as the kitchen. Harvest by shearing the whole plant back by a third periodically to encourage fresh regrowth and prevent flowering, which keeps the leaves at their best flavor. Give it full sun and well-drained soil, and avoid overwatering, which can lead to root problems in its tight, twiggy growth.

planting.note: Set out divisions or nursery plants after the last frost into a contained bed or pot to control its spreading rhizomes.

directions: Chewing Gum mint is a spearmint selection grown for its distinctive sweet, bubblegum-like aroma and flavor layered over a typical minty base, with dark green leaves that often show a mahogany or purplish tint on the stems. Like other spearmints it spreads aggressively by underground runners, so confine it to a pot or a bottomless container sunk in the ground to keep it from overtaking nearby beds. Grow in moist, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, harvesting leaves regularly for teas and flavored drinks, which keeps plants bushy and encourages fresh new growth.

planting.note: Start seed indoors under warmth about a month before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees.

directions: Queenette is a compact Thai basil bred for a smaller, more uniform habit than open-pollinated Thai basil strains, with the same purple stems, purple-tinged olive-green leaves, and spicy anise-clove flavor prized in Southeast Asian cooking. Its thicker leaves hold up well in stir-fries, curries, and simmered soups without turning mushy. Pinch flower spikes regularly to delay bolting and keep the plant producing tender new leaves, and harvest often once it reaches a usable size. Grow in full sun with consistent warmth, since Thai basil is more cold-sensitive than common sweet basil.
